public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 270

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/270](https://www.erdosproblems.com/270)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Ha75] Hansen, E. R., *A Table of Series and Products*. Prentice-Hall (1975), 87.
- [CrKo25] T. Crmarić and V. Kovač, *On the irrationality of certain super-polynomially decaying
  series*. arXiv:2504.18712 (2025).
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter

namespace Erdos270

/-- The series $\sum_{n\geq 1} \frac{1}{(n+1)\cdots (n+f(n))}$, indexed from $0$. -/
noncomputable def series (f : ℕ → ℕ) : ℝ :=
  ∑' n : ℕ, (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc (n + 2) (n + 1 + f (n + 1)), (i : ℝ))⁻¹

/--
Let $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$. Is it true that
$$\sum_{n\geq 1} \frac{1}{(n+1)\cdots (n+f(n))}$$
is irrational?

Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] write 'the answer is almost surely in the affirmative if $f(n)$ is
assumed to be nondecreasing'. Even the case $f(n)=n$ is unknown, although Hansen [Ha75] has
shown that
$$\sum_n \frac{1}{\binom{2n}{n}}=\sum_n \frac{n!}{(n+1)\cdots (n+n)}=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{2\pi}{3^{5/2}}$$
is transcendental.

Crmarić and Kovač [CrKo25] have shown that the answer to this question is no in a strong sense:
for any $\alpha \in (0,\infty)$ there exists a function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that
$f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to\infty$ and
$$\sum_{n\geq 1} \frac{1}{(n+1)\cdots (n+f(n))}=\alpha.$$
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos270.lean#L1027"]
theorem erdos_270 : answer(False) ↔
    ∀ f : ℕ → ℕ, Tendsto f atTop atTop → Irrational (series f) := by
  sorry

/--
Crmarić and Kovač [CrKo25]: for any $\alpha \in (0,\infty)$ there exists a function
$f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to\infty$ and
$$\sum_{n\geq 1} \frac{1}{(n+1)\cdots (n+f(n))}=\alpha.$$
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos270.lean#L1009"]
theorem erdos_270.variants.every_value (α : ℝ) (hα : 0 < α) :
    ∃ f : ℕ → ℕ, Tendsto f atTop atTop ∧
      HasSum (fun n : ℕ => (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc (n + 2) (n + 1 + f (n + 1)), (i : ℝ))⁻¹) α := by
  sorry

/--
It is still possible that this sum is always irrational if $f$ is assumed to be non-decreasing;
Crmarić and Kovač [CrKo25] show that the set of the possible values of such a sum has Lebesgue
measure zero.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_270.variants.monotone : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ f : ℕ → ℕ, Monotone f → Tendsto f atTop atTop → Irrational (series f) := by
  sorry

/-- Even the case $f(n)=n$ is unknown. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_270.variants.linear : answer(sorry) ↔ Irrational (series id) := by
  sorry

end Erdos270

findings.description: The existential ranges over every `f : ℕ → ℕ`, so a witness may vanish at finitely many n ≥ 1. At such an n the product over `Finset.Icc (n+2) (n+1)` is empty and the term is 1. The cited theorem (Crmarić–Kovač, Theorem 1) only allows f with positive-integer values. The Lean claim is therefore implied by the cited result but is a priori weaker. For α ≤ 1 the two coincide: a zero makes the sum exceed 1. For α > 1, witnesses containing terms equal to 1 are accepted, which the source does not allow. I found no argument deriving the positive version from the Lean version, short of redoing the paper's construction. The statement is still true and non-trivial, and the linked formal proof (plby L1009, `erdos_270_resolution`) proves the stronger version with `∀ n, 0 < f n`. So this is a fidelity point, not a false or vacuous statement. The same zero convention is harmless in `erdos_270` and `variants.monotone` (see reformulations).
findings.source_evidence: arXiv:2504.18712 (Crmarić–Kovač), LaTeX source, just before Theorem 1: "Let $\N$ denote the set of positive integers." Theorem 1: "The set { ∑_{n=1}^∞ 1/∏_{i=1}^{f(n)}(n+i) : (f(n))_{n=1}^∞ ∈ ℕ^ℕ, lim f(n) = ∞ } is equal to the whole interval (0,∞)." Abstract: "whenever (f(n)) is a sequence of positive integers converging to infinity". erdosproblems.com/270 paraphrases this as "there exists a function f:ℕ→ℕ such that f(n)→∞ ... and ∑_{n≥1} 1/((n+1)⋯(n+f(n))) = α".
findings.suggested_fix: Require positivity of the witness, as in the linked formal proof: `∃ f : ℕ → ℕ, (∀ n, 0 < f n) ∧ Tendsto f atTop atTop ∧ HasSum (fun n : ℕ => (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc (n + 2) (n + 1 + f (n + 1)), (i : ℝ))⁻¹) α`. Alternatively, require it only for n ≥ 1, since f 0 is unused.

status_issues.recorded: @[category research open, AMS 11] with `answer(sorry) ↔ Irrational (series id)`. The docstring says "Even the case f(n)=n is unknown.", and the same sentence appears in the docstring of `erdos_270`.
status_issues.source_status: Solved in the affirmative: ∑_{n≥1} 1/((n+1)⋯(2n)) = ∑ n!/(2n)! is irrational. Crmarić and Kovač observed this after their paper [CrKo25]. Kovač posted it on the erdosproblems.com forum thread for #270 on 12 Jul 2026, two months before this file was added (commit fce15fc, 2026-09-19). The main text of erdosproblems.com/270 has not yet been updated and still says "Even the case f(n)=n is unknown". The post carries a "main problem discussion needs to be updated" reaction.
status_issues.evidence: erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/270, post-7469 (Vjeko_Kovac, 14:00 on 12 Jul 2026): "Tonći Crmarić and I later (after [CrKo25]) observed that the case f(n)=n, i.e., the first part of the question by Erdős and Graham in [ErGr80], actually has a very simple positive answer. Namely, ∑_{n=1}^∞ 1/((n+1)(n+2)⋯(n+n)) = ∑ n!/(2n)! = 0.592296536… is an irrational number. This is (shamefully) easily seen by writing it as ∑ 1/(a_1 a_2⋯a_n), a_k := 4k−2 … the proof is the same as Fourier's ancient proof of the irrationality of e." I proved this in Lean against the file's own definition. `theorem linear_true : Irrational (Erdos270.series id)` compiles, as does `example : True ↔ Irrational (Erdos270.series id)`, i.e. the file's statement with `answer(True)`. The only axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. Proof sketch (~150 lines): let B n := ∏_{i ∈ Icc (n+2) (2n+2)} i. Then B (n+1) = B n · (4n+6), so B n ∣ B N for n ≤ N, and B N · (tail after N) ≤ 1/(4N+5). If the sum were a/b, then b · B N · tail = a · B N − b · (integer) would be a nonzero integer of absolute value < 1 once 4N+5 > |b|.

In the docstrings of `erdos_270.variants.linear` and `erdos_270`, replace "Even the case f(n)=n is unknown" with a note that this case is irrational by the elementary Fourier/Engel-series argument (Crmarić–Kovač, erdosproblems.com forum, July 2026). reformulations.difference: The right-hand side ranges over every `f : ℕ → ℕ` with `Tendsto f atTop atTop`, so f may vanish at finitely many n; such a term is 1/(empty product) = 1. The source and Crmarić–Kovač take f with positive-integer values.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Since f → ∞, the set of n with f(n+1) = 0 is finite. Replacing f by g = max f 1 changes only those finitely many terms, and each old and new term is the inverse of a natural number, hence rational. If g's series is summable, `series f = series g + r` for some rational r, and irrationality is preserved (`irrational_add_ratCast_iff`). If it is not summable, then neither is f's (they differ by a finitely supported function), both `tsum`s are 0, and both sides of the ↔ are false. g is positive and tends to ∞. So quantifying over all f is equivalent to quantifying over positive f. Proved in Lean (scratch `Test2.main_reform`, axioms propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound).

reformulations.difference: Uses `Monotone f` on all of ℕ, which adds the constraint f 0 ≤ f 1 on a value the series never uses, and allows zero values. The source takes positive-integer f, non-decreasing on n ≥ 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (→) Given positive f, non-decreasing on n ≥ 1, set g 0 := 1 and g n := f n otherwise. Then g is Monotone on ℕ, tends to ∞, and has the same series, because `series` only reads f (n+1). (←) Given Monotone f with zeros, max f 1 is still Monotone and positive, and changes the series by a rational, as for `erdos_270`. Proved in Lean (scratch `Test2.monotone_reform`, axioms propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound).
